Swan River Daisy.why: Flowers through the hot, dry Birak months across the Swan Coastal Plain.
Swan River Daisy.where_to_find: Open woodland and heath across the Swan Coastal Plain.

Rottnest Island Lace Flower.why: Also called the Blue Lace Flower; blooms in sandy coastal areas during the warmer months.
Rottnest Island Lace Flower.where_to_find: Sandy coastal plains and lake margins, e.g. around Rockingham.

Golden Verticordia.why: A feather flower that blooms in the heat of early Birak.
Golden Verticordia.where_to_find: Sandy heathland in the South West.

Jarrah.why: A dominant South West forest tree; its flowering overlaps with the dry Bunuru months.
Jarrah.where_to_find: Jarrah forest across the Darling Range and South West.

Marri.why: A large flowering gum, often paired with jarrah in South West forests, flowering through summer.
Marri.where_to_find: Open forest and woodland across the South West.

Ghost gums.why: A white-barked eucalypt found in the Perth hills, flowering through the warmer months.
Ghost gums.where_to_find: Kalamunda National Park and the Perth Hills.

Djiriji (zamia palm).why: A cycad whose seeds were a traditional food source once properly prepared to remove toxins.
Djiriji (zamia palm).where_to_find: Jarrah and banksia woodland understorey across the South West.

Red-flowering gum.why: One of the most recognisable flowering gums of the South West, blooming as the weather cools into Djeran.
Red-flowering gum.where_to_find: Native to a small area near Walpole, widely planted as a street tree across Perth.

Summer flame.why: A bright red-flowering shrub blooming in late summer into autumn.
Summer flame.where_to_find: Sandy heath and woodland in the South West.

Banksias (Djeran).why: Firewood banksia; one of the first banksias to flower as the weather cools.
Banksias (Djeran).where_to_find: Sandy soils across the Swan Coastal Plain.

Blueberry lily.why: A hardy understorey plant that flowers through the cold, wet Makuru months.
Blueberry lily.where_to_find: Woodland and heath understorey across the South West.

Purple flags.why: A native iris flowering through the wetter winter months.
Purple flags.where_to_find: Damp heath and woodland, South West.

Acacias.scientific_name: Acacia pulchella (prickly moses) and related species
Acacias.why: Wattles are among the first big flowering events of Djilba, as the first wildflowers of the season appear.
Acacias.where_to_find: Woodland and bushland understorey across the South West.

Weeping peppermint (wannang).why: A distinctive weeping-foliage tree of the Swan Coastal Plain, widely used as a street tree in Perth.
Weeping peppermint (wannang).where_to_find: Coastal limestone soils across the Swan Coastal Plain.

Jarrah (Djilba).why: Early jarrah flowering can begin as part of Djilba's major South West flowering period.
Jarrah (Djilba).where_to_find: Jarrah forest across the Darling Range and South West.

Banksias (Kambarang).why: Continues flowering into Kambarang's burst of spring wildflowers.
Banksias (Kambarang).where_to_find: Sandy soils across the Swan Coastal Plain.

Kangaroo paw.why: Western Australia's floral emblem; flowers prolifically through Kambarang.
Kangaroo paw.where_to_find: Sandy bushland and woodland across the South West, notably Kings Park.

Orchids.why: One of many native orchid species that flower through the South West spring.
Orchids.where_to_find: Jarrah and banksia woodland, South West.

Balga.why: The grass tree's tall flower spike is a distinctive sign of the South West spring.
Balga.where_to_find: Woodland and heath across the South West, including Kings Park.

Young birds.why: Birds that bred earlier in the year fledge and leave the nest as Birak begins.
Young birds.where_to_find: Across Perth's woodlands, parks and gardens.

Reptiles shedding skin.scientific_name: Pseudonaja affinis (dugite, pictured) and other local reptiles
Reptiles shedding skin.why: Reptiles become more active in the heat of Birak and shed their skin as they grow.
Reptiles shedding skin.where_to_find: Bushland and reserves across the Perth region.

Dolphins and calves.why: Dolphins are commonly seen close to shore and in the Swan River estuary during the warm Bunuru months.
Dolphins and calves.where_to_find: Swan River estuary and nearshore coastal waters.

Snakes (Bunuru).why: Snakes are most active in the hot, dry Bunuru months.
Snakes (Bunuru).where_to_find: Wetlands and bushland across the South West — note tiger snakes favour wetter southern areas; dugites are more common around Perth itself.

Lizards.why: Large monitor lizards are frequently active and visible during the hot Bunuru season.
Lizards.where_to_find: Bushland and sandy areas across the Perth region.

Flying ants.why: Winged ants emerge in swarms as the weather cools and the first rains return in Djeran.
Flying ants.where_to_find: Gardens, parks and bushland across Perth.

Black swans (Mali).why: Black swans gather on lakes and rivers to prepare for nesting and breeding during Makuru.
Black swans (Mali).where_to_find: Swan River, Lake Monger and other Perth wetlands.

Koolbardi, Djidi djidi and chuck-a-luck.scientific_name: Gymnorhina tibicen (magpie, pictured), Rhipidura leucophrys (willy wagtail), Anthochaera spp. (wattlebird)
Koolbardi, Djidi djidi and chuck-a-luck.why: These birds are protective of their young during Djilba's major breeding season.
Koolbardi, Djidi djidi and chuck-a-luck.where_to_find: Parks, gardens and woodland across Perth.

Snakes and reptiles (Kambarang).scientific_name: various species, e.g. Tiliqua rugosa (bobtail, pictured)
Snakes and reptiles (Kambarang).why: Reptiles emerge from winter dormancy as temperatures rise in Kambarang.
Snakes and reptiles (Kambarang).where_to_find: Bushland, parks and gardens across the Perth region.

Blue swimmer crab.why: A traditional coastal food source as Noongar people moved toward the coast during Birak.
Blue swimmer crab.where_to_find: Estuaries and shallow coastal waters, e.g. Swan River and Cockburn Sound.

Gilgies.why: A freshwater crayfish traditionally caught from rivers and wetlands during the warmer months.
Gilgies.where_to_find: Freshwater streams, wetlands and rivers across the South West.

Freshwater turtle.why: A traditional food source from freshwater wetlands as the wetter months of Djeran begin.
Freshwater turtle.where_to_find: Wetlands, rivers and lakes across the Perth region.

Kangaroo (yongar).why: A traditional land-based food source as the focus shifts inland during the cold, wet Makuru season.
Kangaroo (yongar).where_to_find: Woodland and bushland across the South West.

Emu (waitj).why: A traditional food source during Djilba, alongside kangaroo and possum.
Emu (waitj).where_to_find: Open woodland and bushland across the South West.

Quandong.why: A native peach eaten as a traditional food, fruiting through spring.
Quandong.where_to_find: Semi-arid woodland and bushland across WA.
